q: Which of the following is the lecture's definition of 'failure'?
options: a regularly interacting or interdependent group of items forming a unified whole
the inability of a system to meet its stakeholders' requirements
the end of a project within budget and time
the state or condition of not meeting a desirable or intended objective
explain: Failure - the state or condition of not meeting a desirable or intended objective. The second option defines 'system'.

q: Which type of failure is when an information system project cannot be developed within an allocated budget and/or time schedule?
explain: Process failure is when an information system project cannot be developed within an allocated budget, the time schedule, or both.

q: Which type of failure is when the objectives/goals of the systems design are not met?
explain: Correspondence failure is when the objectives or goals of the systems design are not met.

q: Which type of failure is attributed to the level of end-user usage, adoption or acceptance of the implemented information system?
explain: Interaction failure is attributed to the level of end-user usage, adoption or acceptance of the implemented information system.

q: Which type of failure is the inability of a system to meet its stakeholders' requirements, expectations or values?
explain: Expectation failure is the inability of a system to meet its stakeholders' requirements, expectations or values.

q: Which type of system failure is the failure of one or more components that renders the system irrecoverable?
explain: Catastrophic - failure of one or more components that renders the system irrecoverable.

q: Which type of system failure is the failure of one or more components that impedes the operation of a system?
explain: Partial - failure of one or more components to impede the operation of a system.

q: Which type of system failure causes a system to stop working temporarily or permanently?
explain: Total - failure of one or more components that causes a system to stop working temporarily or permanently.

q: In the 'Normal Accident' idea, what does complexity plus tight interaction give?
explain: In the "Normal Accident" idea, complexity plus tight interaction gives catastrophic potential.

q: What does 'tightly coupled' mean?
options: interacting elements with no 'buffer' or delay possible
there are multiple routes between elements
elements are backed up with dissimilar systems
explain: Tightly coupled means interacting elements with no "buffer" or delay possible. Linear means one thing then another, and complex means multiple routes.

q: How many primary reasons for system failures does the lecture ask you to recall?
explain: The learning objective is to recall the six primary reasons for system failures.

q: How many types of system failure does the lecture give?
explain: The types of system failure are Partial, Total and Catastrophic.

q: How many classifications of system failure does the lecture give?
explain: Classification of system failures lists process, correspondence, interaction and expectation failure.

q: Which statement below is NOT correct for safety critical systems?
options: graceful degradation on failure of sub-system
rigorous external independent oversight of specification, design, testing, approval, implementation, operation processes and maintenance
explain: Safety critical systems need multiple backups using dissimilar systems/hardware/software, not similar.

q: On what date did the Kegworth air crash flight take off from Heathrow?
explain: On the evening of 8th January 1989, British Midland Airways flight BD092 took off from Heathrow.

q: Which aircraft was involved in the Kegworth air crash?
explain: British Midland Airways flight BD092 was a Boeing 737-400.

q: In the Kegworth air crash, in which engine had a fan blade fractured?
explain: Unbeknown to the crew, a fan blade in engine #1 had fractured. The first officer wrongly replied engine #2, which was throttled back.

q: Where did the Kegworth flight crash?
options: onto the runway at East Midlands Airport
explain: The plane was cleared for an emergency landing at East Midlands Airport but crashed into the M1 motorway.

q: According to the lecture, how many of the passengers on board were lost in the Kegworth crash?
explain: The slide says the crash resulted in the loss of 47 of the 126 passengers on board.
flag: The slide says 47 of the 126 "passengers on board" and does not mention crew.

q: On what date did the Three Mile Island failure occur?
explain: On the morning of 28th March 1979 the secondary, non-nuclear part of Three Mile Island experienced a mechanical failure.

q: What was the first failure in the chain of events at Three Mile Island?
options: a mechanical failure causing the main-feed water pump to stop running
a power cut at the control room
the relief valve being closed by mistake
explain: A mechanical failure caused the main-feed water pump to stop running, firing a chain of events ending in partial nuclear meltdown.

q: Is the following statement correct? 'At Three Mile Island, the light indicating the relief valve position reflected the actual state of the valve.'
explain: The light only reflected the command sent, not the valve state.

q: How many people suffered massive radiation overdoses because of the Therac-25 software bug?
explain: Therac-25 ... massive radiation overdoses being administered to 6 people.

q: What software problem caused the Therac-25 mechanical interlock to fail?
explain: A software "race condition" made the mechanical interlock fail. That interlock applies the x-ray filter.

q: In the Therac-25 session described, how many times was the process repeated with 'NO DOSE' showing?
explain: The process was repeated 4 times, and each time it showed "NO DOSE".
flag: The slide text is "This process was repeated 4 times". It does not say whether the first press counts.

q: Is the following statement correct? 'Failures due to a lack of training are not errors, they are mistakes by management.'
explain: Slide on inadequate user training states exactly that.
flag: Same slide also says incorrect data input from a bad interface 'can be considered errors'.

q: Which statement below is NOT correct?
options: It is difficult to guard against faulty hardware
There is no excuse for faulty code
If the interface is poorly designed, user errors get introduced
Bad training = loss of data integrity
It is easy to guard against faulty hardware
explain: The Faulty Hardware slide says it is difficult to guard against faulty hardware and there is no excuse for faulty code.

q: Which of these is NOT given as a reason for information system implementation?
options: to increase productivity in order to maintain competitive advantage
to reduce the number of stakeholders
to re-engineer a process for efficiency
adapt to a change in existing process
explain: The four reasons are increase productivity, re-engineer a process, adapt to a change in existing process, introduce a new process.

q: According to the lecture, what is a poor fit between system and organisation often driven by?
explain: A poor fit between system and organisation is often driven by cost and poor specification.

q: What does the lecture say about the 'Incorrect Assumptions' cause?
options: development team guess, or don't check
explain: Under Incorrect Assumptions, the development team guess or don't check.

q: What are the causes of system failures?
options: poor fit between system and organisation
explain: The six causes are poor development practices, incorrect assumptions, poor user interface, faulty hardware, inadequate user training, and poor fit between system and organisation. All five options are on the list.

q: Which of the following are causes of system failures?
explain: The listed causes are poor development practices, incorrect assumptions, poor user interface, faulty hardware, inadequate user training, and poor fit between system and organisation.

q: What actions could reduce or prevent system failures?
options: rigorous external independent oversight of specification and design
graceful degradation on failure of sub-system
explain: Backups should use dissimilar systems/hardware/software. The other four are on the safety critical systems slide.

q: Safety critical systems should have rigorous external independent oversight of which of the following?
explain: All seven are listed under rigorous external independent oversight.

q: What would be the main reasons for system failure?
options: no clear responsibility for dealing with failure
large projects have a momentum of their own
organisational culture such as unreasonable deadlines
explain: The reasons for failure are people, meaning poor training, not following procedures and stress, organisational culture such as unreasonable deadlines, no clear responsibility, and large projects having a momentum of their own. Dissimilar backups are a prevention.

q: Which are listed under organisational culture as reasons for failure?
options: too expensive to contemplate (failure scenario / remedy)
blame / aggressive leadership who can't be queried
explain: Organisational culture lists blame/aggressive leadership, pressure/unreasonable/political deadlines, too expensive to contemplate, top management kept in dark.

q: Which are listed under 'People' as reasons for failure?
options: not following procedures before / during / after
explain: Under People, the slide lists poor training, not following procedures before, during and after, and stress and pressure before, during and after.

q: Under 'no clear responsibility for dealing with failure', which points are given?
options: blame / aggressive leadership who can't be queried
explain: The three bullets under no clear responsibility are different agendas/cover-up, who pays, unwillingness to take legal responsibility.

q: Which of the following are classifications of system failure?
explain: The classifications are process, correspondence, interaction and expectation failure. Partial, total and catastrophic are the types.

q: Which of the following are types of system failure?
explain: The types are Partial, Total and Catastrophic. The other options are classifications.

q: What are the stated reasons for information system implementation?
options: adapt to a change in existing process
to increase productivity in order to maintain competitive advantage
to re-engineer a process for efficiency
explain: All four appear on the slide.

q: According to the lecture, failure is costly in which ways?
explain: Failure is costly through loss of money, loss of reputation or job, and possibly loss of life.

q: Complexity of projects means which of the following under poor development practices?
explain: Under Poor Development Practices, complexity of projects means poor specification, poor design and poor testing.

q: Which statements about the Kegworth air crash are correct?
options: The plane crashed into the M1 motorway
A fan blade in engine #1 had fractured
The flight was British Midland Airways BD092
The plane crashed into the M25
A fan blade in engine #2 had fractured
explain: The slide says flight BD092 was a Boeing 737-400, a fan blade in engine #1 fractured, and the plane crashed into the M1.

q: Which actions occurred in the Kegworth air crash?
options: the plane landed safely at Heathrow
the captain asked the first officer which engine was causing the problem
the plane was cleared for an emergency landing at East Midlands Airport
the first officer replied engine #2 after some hesitation
the captain took the plane off autopilot
explain: The slide says the captain followed procedure, the first officer replied engine #2 after hesitation, engine #2 was throttled back, the plane was cleared for East Midlands, and it crashed into the M1.

q: Which statements about the Three Mile Island failure are correct?
options: The pilot-operated relief valve remained open
The main-feed water pump stopped running
The failure was caused by a software race condition
The indicator light only reflected the command sent to the valve
The auxiliary water feeds were shut for maintenance
explain: The slide says the main-feed water pump stopped, the auxiliary feeds were shut for maintenance, the relief valve stuck open, and the indicator showed the command, not the state. The race condition belongs to Therac-25.

q: Which statements about Three Mile Island are correct?
options: An operator triggered the pilot-operated relief valve to relieve system pressure
It ended in partial nuclear meltdown
The failure began in the secondary, non-nuclear part
It happened on the morning of 28th March 1979
explain: The slide gives the morning of 28th March 1979, the secondary non-nuclear part, a partial nuclear meltdown, and an operator triggering the valve to relieve pressure.

q: Which statements about Therac-25 are correct?
options: It was caused by a faulty hardware sensor
The mechanical interlock applies the x-ray filter
A software race condition caused the mechanical interlock to fail
The overdoses were recorded correctly each time
It is a radiation therapy machine
Massive radiation overdoses were administered to 6 people
explain: The slide says it is a radiation therapy machine, a race condition was involved, the interlock applies the x-ray filter, the number of people is 6, and the dose would not be recorded.

q: Which details are given about the Therac-25 therapy session?
options: the patient made a full recovery
the patient complained of a burning sensation in her hip
the patient died a month later of the cancer
explain: The slide says the machine paused with HTILT, NO DOSE was shown, the operator pressed proceed, the patient felt a burning sensation in her hip, and she died a month later.

q: Which statements about inadequate user training are correct?
options: Failures due to lack of training are user errors, not management's fault
Failures due to lack of training are mistakes by management
Improper training increases the likelihood of serious errors
Bad training = loss of data integrity
Training has no effect on data integrity
explain: The slide says lack of knowledge increases serious errors, bad training means loss of data integrity, and such failures are mistakes by management.

q: Which statements about the 'Normal Accident' idea are correct?
options: linear is simple, one thing then another
tightly coupled means no 'buffer' or delay possible
explain: All four are on the Normal Accident slide.

q: Which cause-case study pairings match the lecture?
options: Kegworth - the wrong engine was throttled back
Three Mile Island - relief valve stuck open
Three Mile Island - software race condition
explain: In Kegworth, engine #2 was throttled back. At Three Mile Island, the valve stayed open and the main-feed water pump failed. In Therac-25, the cause was a race condition.

q: Which statements about the lecture's definitions are correct?
options: A failure is a group of items forming a unified whole
A system is a regularly interacting or interdependent group of items forming a unified whole
A failure is the state or condition of not meeting a desirable or intended objective
A system is the state or condition of not meeting an intended objective
explain: A system is a regularly interacting or interdependent group of items forming a unified whole. A failure is the state or condition of not meeting a desirable or intended objective.

q: Which of the following are listed among the reasons for failure?
options: large projects have a momentum of their own
explain: Slide 20 lists these reasons. Rigorous testing is a prevention on slide 19.

q: What are the stated learning objectives of the system failures lecture?
options: recall the six primary reasons for system failures
explain: All four objectives are on the slide.

q: Which of these are listed on the Why do I care? slide?
options: Some of you will manage projects - beware of why they fail
You will all be involved in delivery projects - many will fail
explain: Slide 21 lists those three points. Failure costs money, reputation or job, and possibly life.

q: Which statements about the system failure causes 'poor user interface' and 'faulty hardware' are correct?
options: Faulty hardware is easy to guard against
A poor interface never affects data input
If the interface is poorly designed, user errors get introduced
It is difficult to guard against faulty hardware
There is no excuse for faulty code
explain: Slides 13 to 14 say a poorly designed interface introduces user errors, it is difficult to guard against faulty hardware, and there is no excuse for faulty code.
